question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
# Notice to vacate after asking for repairs: periodic tenancy, 1 November 2019

**Short answer:** On 1 November 2019 the version in force was Authorised Version 088 of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf, dated 2 July 2019), which applied from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The parts of Version 088 I found don't include the main anti-retaliation rule for ordinary tenancies (s 266(2)) or the rule for no-reason notices (s 263). Those sections only appear in later versions, so I can't confirm their exact wording on your date.

---

## What the law says

**From Version 088 (in force on your date):**
- If you get a no-reason notice under s 263, s 237 lets you leave sooner. You can give a notice of intention to vacate with a termination date at least **14 days** after you give it [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The anti-retaliation rule I found in Version 088 is for **rooming houses** only. A no-reason notice under s 288 "is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the resident of a right under this Act." It can't be challenged more than **60 days** after it was given [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This only helps you if you live in a rooming house.

**Only found in later versions (Version 090, in force from 2 March 2020, and Version 097, dated 28 March 2021):**
- **s 266(2):** a notice under s 261 or s 263 "is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the tenant of a right under this Act" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).
- **s 266(3)(c):** you can't apply to the Tribunal to challenge a s 263 notice "after the end of 60 days after the date on which the notice is given" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).
- **s 263:** a landlord can give notice without a reason. For a periodic tenancy, the termination date must be at least **120 days** after the notice is given, or a prescribed period if one is set [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).
- **s 265:** a landlord can't give a s 263 notice while an excessive-rent order under s 47 is in force [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).

Version 088 has a margin note just before s 268 saying s 266(3)(c) was amended by No. 45/2002. That suggests s 266 already existed on your date [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), but I couldn't find its text in Version 088.

---

## What to check and ask

1. **Which section the notice relies on.** The later s 266(2) only protects against **s 261 or s 263** notices [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). If the notice gives a reason, check that the reason is real. For example, a repairs notice under s 255 needs the landlord to intend the work, to have all permits and consents, and the work must be impossible to do with you living there. It also needs at least **60 days'** notice [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
2. **The termination date.** For a no-reason notice on a periodic tenancy, check it gives at least **120 days** (based on later versions) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Evidence of timing.** Keep your repair requests and the notice, since they arrived on the same day. Under the later text, the question is whether the notice was given "in response to" you using a right under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).
4. **The deadline.** If you want to challenge a s 263 notice, apply to the Tribunal within **60 days** of receiving it (based on later versions) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).
5. **The repairs themselves.** The repair sections (ss 72–77) only appear in the version from 4 December 2019, not in what I found from Version 088 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). In that version:
   - You can apply to the Tribunal for urgent repairs, and it must hear you within **2 business days**.
   - For non-urgent repairs, if the landlord hasn't fixed things within **14 days** of your written notice, you can ask the Director to investigate.
   - You can apply to pay rent into the Rent Special Account [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).

Before relying on s 263 or s 266, check the full text of Version 088. Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service can also help you.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are stated, and the caveats about relying on later versions do not leave the direction unclear. The answer says a s 263 no-reason notice on a periodic tenancy needs a termination date 'at least 120 days after the notice is given'. It says the notice 'is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the tenant of a right under this Act', which it ties to the repair requests. It also tells the tenant to 'apply to the Tribunal within 60 days of receiving it'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer states "a landlord can give notice without a reason" (s 263) and gives only a 60-day challenge deadline ("apply to the Tribunal within **60 days** of receiving it"); its other periods (14, 120, 2 business days) are for vacating, notice length and repairs, not for challenging the notice at VCAT.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names 'Authorised Version 088 of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf, dated 2 July 2019)' as the version in force, but it relies on versions that were not. It presents s 266(2), the 120-day period and the 60-day challenge deadline from Version 090 and Version 097 as steps the user can take, and gives repair remedies from the version dated 4 December 2019 (97-109aa089). Deleting everything sourced from those versions would substantially change the answer's substance.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Short answer:** Possibly, but it depends on how the higher offer came about. On 1 October 2025 it was an offence for the agent or landlord to ask for or invite an offer above the advertised rent. It was **not yet** an offence for them to accept a higher offer that someone made on their own initiative. That ban started on 25 November 2025.

**Law in force on 1 October 2025:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version 110** (rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf), in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

---

### What the law says

**Rental bidding (s 30F)**
- The landlord or agent must advertise or offer the property at a fixed rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- They must not "solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount of rent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The penalty for each is 60 penalty units for an individual and 300 penalty units for a company [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**If the other person offered more without being asked**
- In Version 110, s 30F has only subsections (1)–(3). None of them bans accepting a higher offer that wasn't asked for [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- That ban is s 30F(4), inserted by No. 6/2025 s 7. It appears only in the later **Authorised Version 111** (rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf), in force from 25 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). It doesn't apply to what happened to you.

**Misleading statements about rent (s 30G)**
- A landlord or agent who advertises a property "must not make a false or misleading representation in relation to the rent," with the same penalties [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- This section applies only to a landlord who is not acting in trade or commerce, and to that landlord's agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**The higher rent in the new listing**
- Nothing in Version 110 stops a landlord from re-advertising at a higher rent, as long as it is a fixed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**The email saying you withdrew**
- I couldn't find anything in the documents that deals directly with an agent falsely saying an applicant withdrew.
- Section 30E (misleading conduct) only covers conduct used to persuade someone to *enter* a rental agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It doesn't clearly fit your situation.

**Compensation through the Tribunal**
- The general compensation section, s 210, is for people who are parties to a residential rental agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You never signed one.
- The applicant compensation section, s 210AA, only covers discrimination under s 30A [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You haven't said that applies.
- So the documents don't show a clear way for you to claim compensation. The main relevant rule is the s 30F(3) offence.

---

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the agent in writing:**
   - Why was your application recorded as withdrawn?
   - Did they ask for, or invite, offers above the advertised rent?
2. **Find out how the higher offer happened.** If the agent invited it (for example, by asking applicants to "make your best offer"), that may breach s 30F(3) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If the other person offered more unprompted, Version 110 doesn't make accepting it an offence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Reporting it:** Version 110 doesn't say who to report a breach to. The only contact I found is Consumer Affairs Victoria (consumer.vic.gov.au, 1300 55 81 81). It's printed on the standard application form in a **later** document: *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Version 005, in force from 25 November 2025 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That form wasn't in force on 1 October 2025.

### What to save as evidence

The documents don't list what evidence to keep. Based on what the law above requires someone to prove, I'd keep:
- **The original ad** showing the fixed rent (screenshots with the date and web address). This goes to s 30F(1) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **The new listing** at the higher rent, also with the date.
- **Your application** and any confirmation you got that it was received.
- **The "withdrawn" email in full**, including the sender, date and time, plus proof you never withdrew (for example, your sent emails).
- **Anything showing the agent invited higher offers**, such as messages, ad wording or notes from calls. This is the key evidence for s 30F(3) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Details of how you heard about the higher offer**: who told you, when, and exactly what they said.
- **Notes on every conversation** with the agent: date, time, who you spoke to and what was said.

This summary is based only on the documents I found. For advice on your specific situation, contact a tenancy advice service or a lawyer.

The output covers all four points: re-advertising at a higher fixed rent is allowed ('Nothing in Version 110 stops a landlord from re-advertising at a higher rent, as long as it is a fixed amount'), soliciting or inviting higher offers is banned under s 30F, accepting an unsolicited higher offer was not banned until 25 November 2025, and on the hardest point, the false withdrawal email, it says 'I couldn't find anything in the documents that deals directly with an agent falsely saying an applicant withdrew.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failing claims is asserted. The answer says "Nothing in Version 110 stops a landlord from re-advertising at a higher rent" and that on 1 October 2025 "It was **not yet** an offence for them to accept a higher offer that someone made on their own initiative," and it never suggests the applicant can force the agent to rent the property to them.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer correctly names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110 (rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf)' and properly treats Version 111 only as later law. However, it relies on 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Version 005, in force from 25 November 2025' (21-3sra005) for the Consumer Affairs Victoria reporting step it gives the user, and that version was not in force on 1 October 2025 (Version 004 was). Presenting this as a step the user can take counts as relying on it despite the caveat, and deleting it would change the substance of the 'Reporting it' advice.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
# Can the owner refuse your dog because of their allergy?

**Short answer:** Only if the owner applied to VCAT within 14 days of getting your request. An agent saying no is not enough. Three weeks have passed, so if nobody applied to VCAT, the law treats the owner as having agreed.

**Version applied:** For 15 October 2026 I used *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, **Authorised Version No. 115**, which includes amendments up to 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The pet rules (sections 71A–71E) say the same thing in the earlier Version No. 111 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

---

## What the law says

- **You need consent or a VCAT order.** You can keep a pet if the owner has agreed in writing or VCAT has made an order allowing it (s 71A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **You have to use the official form.** Your request must be in the form approved by the Director and given to the owner (s 71B) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You say you used the official form. The documents don't say whether giving it to the agent counts as giving it to the owner.
- **The owner can't refuse unreasonably.** The owner "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" (s 71C(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard rental agreement form in the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 says the same thing (*rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf*, Form 1, item 30) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **There's a 14-day deadline.** The owner "is taken to have consented" unless, **within 14 days** after getting your request, they apply to VCAT under s 71D (s 71C(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Saying no, whether directly or through the agent, doesn't stop this deadline from running. Only a VCAT application does.

**About the allergy:** Only VCAT decides whether a refusal is reasonable. When it decides, it can consider:
- the type of pet
- what the property is like
- the appliances, fixtures and fittings
- whether any law allows the refusal
- any prescribed matters
- "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant" (s 71E(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents don't say whether an owner's allergy counts as a reasonable reason when the owner hardly visits. That would be VCAT's decision, so I can't predict how it would go.

---

## What you can do

1. **Ask the agent in writing whether the owner applied to VCAT, and on what date.** It's 21 days since your request. If no application was made within 14 days, the owner is taken to have agreed (s 71C(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **If an application was made in time,** VCAT will decide. It can make an order allowing you to keep the dog. It can also find the refusal reasonable and order that the pet be kept out of the property (s 71E(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). At the hearing, you can point out that the owner rarely visits and give any other relevant facts.
3. **Keep a record** of when and how you gave the request, since the 14 days start from that date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Know the risk if you lose at VCAT.** If VCAT orders the pet out and you haven't followed the order after at least 14 days, the owner can give you a notice to vacate. The notice must give you at least 28 days (s 91ZZG). I found this wording in Version No. 111 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Version No. 115 lists s 91ZZG in its contents [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), but I didn't find its full text in that version.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The output says the owner 'is taken to have consented' unless they apply to VCAT 'within 14 days' after getting the request (s 71C(2)). (2) The hardest point, the application to the three-week facts, is covered by 'Three weeks have passed, so if nobody applied to VCAT, the law treats the owner as having agreed.' (3) The next step is given as 'Ask the agent in writing whether the owner applied to VCAT, and on what date.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the failing claims is asserted, since the answer says "An agent saying no is not enough," puts the VCAT application on the owner ("unless, within 14 days after getting your request, they apply to VCAT"), and treats the allergy as undecided ("That would be VCAT's decision, so I can't predict how it would go").

However, step 4 sets out the s 91ZZG notice-to-vacate rule (at least 28 days) as a risk the user faces, while stating 'I found this wording in Version No. 111'. That relies on a version not in force on 15 October 2026. Deleting it would remove a substantive step from the answer, and the caveat does not cure this.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
## Short answer

**Probably yes, unless the landlord formally withdraws the notice or you get it declared invalid.** A buyer pulling out doesn't automatically cancel a notice to vacate.

**Law applied:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 110 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025). It was in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025, so it covers 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

---

## What the law says

**1. A notice is withdrawn only by a formal notice of withdrawal.** A notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." That withdrawal must be:
- in writing,
- signed by the person who gave the notice, **and**
- signed by the person who received it (you) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

The Act sets no rule that a notice ends because a sale fell through. A notice you have not both signed away still stands [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**2. The "sale" ground has more than one form.** Under s 91ZZB a landlord can give notice to vacate if [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf):
- **(1)** the premises are, immediately after the termination date, "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession", or
- **(2)/(3)** the landlord has signed a contract of sale. The notice must then be given within 14 days after the contract is signed, or within 14 days after the contract's last condition is met.

If your notice relied on a particular contract, losing that buyer may weaken the stated reason. If it relied on the premises being *offered for sale* with vacant possession, the reason may still apply if the landlord plans to keep marketing the property. The documents don't say how a tribunal would decide this.

**3. Notice period.** A sale notice must give a termination date **not less than 60 days** after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). (This rose to 90 days only in a later version, from 25 November 2025 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). That version doesn't apply to you.)

---

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask for a written withdrawal.** Ask the landlord or agent to sign a notice of withdrawal, then sign it yourself. That is the only way the notice is withdrawn [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Check that the notice is valid.** It is invalid unless it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf):
  - is in the prescribed form,
  - is addressed to you,
  - is signed by the landlord or their agent,
  - states the reason,
  - specifies the termination date, **and**
  - comes with documentary evidence supporting the sale reason.
- **If you have a fixed-term lease:** a sale notice has no effect if its termination date is earlier than the end of your term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Discrimination:** the notice has no effect if giving it would be direct discrimination under the *Equal Opportunity Act 2010* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Challenge it at the Tribunal.** You can apply to challenge a s 91ZZB notice, but you must apply **within 30 days after the notice was given** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Act quickly if you're still inside that window.
- **If you leave:** after you leave under a sale notice, the landlord must not re-let the property as a home for **6 months** after the notice date, unless the Tribunal allows it. The penalty is up to **150 penalty units** for an individual or **750** for a company [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

---

**Gap in the documents:** they don't explain what happens if you're still there after the termination date, beyond a reference to possession order hearings [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service can tell you about that stage and how a tribunal might treat a sale that fell through.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The hardest one, that the outcome depends on the ground stated, is met by 'If your notice relied on a particular contract, losing that buyer may weaken the stated reason. If it relied on the premises being *offered for sale* with vacant possession, the reason may still apply', together with the requirement for 'documentary evidence supporting the sale reason'. The answer also states the 60-day minimum, that withdrawal must be in writing and signed by both parties, and next steps including a signed written withdrawal and a Tribunal challenge within 30 days.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the failing claims are made, since the answer says "A buyer pulling out doesn't automatically cancel a notice to vacate", requires a withdrawal "signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person who received it (you)", and gives the period as "not less than 60 days", mentioning 90 days only as a later version that "doesn't apply to you."

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025)' and applies only rules from that version; the later version (97-109aa111) is mentioned only to say the 90-day period starts from 25 November 2025 and doesn't apply, so removing it would not change the substance.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**No. As of 1 October 2025, an email saying the rent is going up isn't enough on its own. You don't have to pay the higher rent until you get a valid notice in the prescribed form, and the increase can only start at least 60 days after that notice is given.**

**Law in force on 1 October 2025:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 110 (rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf), in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

---

## What the law says

- **Notice is required.** Your rental provider must give you **at least 60 days notice in the prescribed form** of a proposed rent increase (s 44(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **What the notice must include** (s 44(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf):
  - the amount of the increase
  - how the increase was calculated
  - a statement that you can ask the Director (Consumer Affairs Victoria) to investigate the proposed rent **within 30 days** after the notice is given
- **One increase per notice** (s 44(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Fixed-term agreements:** the rent can't go up before the term ends unless your agreement allows an increase during the term. Even then, it can't exceed the amount or method stated in the agreement (s 44(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Once every 12 months:** the rent can't go up more often than once every 12 months (s 44(4A)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Breaking these rules makes the increase invalid:** "A rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid" (s 44(5)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Do you have to pay?** An informal email is only a valid notice if it actually meets the s 44 requirements: the prescribed form, at least 60 days notice and the required details [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If it doesn't, the increase is invalid and you can keep paying your current rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Your failed attempt to negotiate doesn't change this. What matters is whether a valid notice was given.

**From when?** No earlier than **60 days after a valid notice is given** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The 12-month limit and any fixed-term rules also apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**About email delivery:** the prescribed agreement form says notices can only be served by email if you consented. It also says that replying to an email doesn't count as consenting [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). That text comes from Form 2 in the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Version 004 (rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf), which is the form for agreements longer than 5 years [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The search results didn't include the Act's general service rules for your type of agreement.

> ⚠️ **Later law doesn't apply to you.** From 25 November 2025, Version No. 111 of the Act and Version 005 of the Regulations (Form 5) require **90 days** notice [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). That isn't the law on 1 October 2025.

---

## What you can do

1. **Ask the agent for a formal notice in the prescribed form.** Check it shows the amount, how it was calculated, the start date (at least 60 days away) and your right to ask the Director to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Keep paying your current rent** until you receive a valid notice and its start date arrives [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check your agreement and payment history.** Find out whether you're on a fixed term and whether the rent has gone up in the last 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **If you think the new rent is too high** once you get a valid notice:
   - Apply **in writing within 30 days** to the Director to investigate (s 45(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
   - After you get the Director's report, you can apply to VCAT **within 30 days** (s 46(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
   - Or, after 30 days have passed, you can apply to VCAT directly with leave. VCAT must be satisfied you had reasonable grounds for not asking the Director first (s 46(3)–(5)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Gaps in the documents:** the search results don't include the version 004 Regulations' rent increase form (Form 5) or the Act's section on paying increased rent while a VCAT decision is pending. So I can't confirm from them what you'd have to pay while a challenge is underway.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
# Dog damage to skirting boards (Victoria, as at 15 October 2026)

**Short answer:** No. You can arrange the repair, but you can't legally keep the damage from the owner. You must tell them in writing. The documents don't say anything about the owner's insurance.

**Which law applies:** On 15 October 2026 the version in force is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 009 (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

---

## What the law says

- **Damage:** You and your visitors must not cause damage to the property on purpose or through carelessness (negligence). Normal wear and tear doesn't count as damage (s 61) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether chewed skirting boards count as careless damage would depend on the facts. The Act doesn't mention pet damage specifically.
- **You must report it in writing (s 62):** As soon as practicable after you notice damage, you must give the owner (the "rental provider") written notice that it happened and what it is. Email or other electronic notice is fine [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Section 72AA repeats this duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard lease summary in the Regulations also says that when damage occurs, "the renter must notify the rental provider in writing" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Fixing the damage doesn't cancel this duty.
- **Who can do repairs:** "Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs—both urgent and non-urgent" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A quick fix by an unqualified handyperson may not meet this standard.
- **When you move out (s 63(2)):** You must leave the property reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Consequences:** These are "duty provisions", so a breach can be dealt with under Part 5 of the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Owner's repair notice:** In the earlier Version No. 111 (in force 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026), ss 78–79 let the owner give a written repair notice. The notice either gives you 14 days to repair the damage at your cost, or says the owner will do it and you pay the reasonable cost within 14 days of completion [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The excerpt of Version No. 115 I found cuts off before s 78, so I can't confirm the current wording from that document.

## What you can do

1. **Tell the owner or agent in writing now**, describing the damage. Email works [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Offer to fix it** with a suitably qualified tradesperson [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), and get the owner's agreement in writing before the work starts.
3. **Keep records:** take before and after photos and keep the invoice. This helps show the property is back in its original condition when you leave [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check your pet consent:** you can keep a pet if the owner agreed in writing or the Tribunal (VCAT) made an order allowing it (s 71A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Make sure you have one of these.

## Insurance

**The documents don't cover this.** Neither the Act nor the Regulations mention the owner's insurance, so I can't say whether a repair would affect their policy. Ask the owner or agent, or check the insurer's terms.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The hardest is renter responsibility, since the answer hedges on whether chewing counts as careless damage under s 61. It is still covered by: 'You must leave the property reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear' (s 63(2)) and 'Normal wear and tear doesn't count as damage'. The answer also gives written notice 'as soon as practicable' (s 62), says 'Neither the Act nor the Regulations mention the owner's insurance', and suggests the next step 'Tell the owner or agent in writing now' and 'Offer to fix it'.

You must tell them in writing'), states no insurance outcome as fact ('I can't say whether a repair would affect their policy'), and never says the renter must pay the owner's insurance excess.

That rule appears under 'What the law says' as a mechanism the owner can use, so it is relied on despite the caveat, and deleting it would change the answer's substance.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** No. On 1 March 2023, the retrieved documents had no rule on how many circuits a rental needs. The electrical safety rule they do contain had not started yet, and it covers what the circuits connect to, not how many there are.

**Version applied:** *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, S.R. No. 3/2021, **Authorised Version 002** (file "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf", dated 1 June 2022). This version was in force from 1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024, so it covers 1 March 2023 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

---

### What the law says

- **No minimum number of circuits.** The electrical safety standard is Schedule 4, clause 9. It only requires that "all power outlets and lighting circuits in the rented premises are to be connected to" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf):
  - (a) "a switchboard-type Circuit Breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000, 'Electrical Installations'"; and
  - (b) "a switchboard-type Residual Current Device" that complies with AS/NZS 3190, AS/NZS 61008.1 or AS/NZS 61009.1 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **That rule wasn't in force yet.** Clause 9 applies "On and from 29 March 2023" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). On 1 March 2023 it was still 28 days away. Even after that date, it doesn't require more circuits or spreading outlets across circuits.
- **General duty to maintain.** The rental provider "must maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask for

1. **Ask when the last electrical safety check was done.** The rental provider must have a licensed or registered electrician check "all electrical installations, appliances and fittings provided by a rental provider" every 2 years. They must give you the date of the most recent check in writing if you ask. If no check was done in the 2 years before you moved in, they must arrange one "as soon as practicable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Report the problem in writing.** You must tell the rental provider in writing, as soon as practicable, about a breakdown of facilities, fixtures or equipment they supplied [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Non-urgent repairs.** The rental provider must carry these out within a reasonable time. If they haven't done the repairs within 14 days of getting your notice, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Urgent repairs.** These are defined in section 3(1) of the Act. They include "failure or breakdown of any essential service or appliance provided for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering supplied by the rental provider" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If the rental provider doesn't act, you can arrange the repairs yourself and be reimbursed up to $2500. You can apply to VCAT if you can't afford the repairs, they cost more than $2500, or the provider refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't include the full section 3(1) list, so they don't say whether a tripping circuit counts as an urgent repair.
5. **Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs**, whether urgent or not [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). That means an electrician, not you.
6. **From 29 March 2023**, you could also ask the rental provider to confirm that every power outlet and lighting circuit is connected to a compliant switchboard circuit breaker and RCD under clause 9 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

### Gaps in the documents

- **Getting a copy of the electrical check report.** The rule that a copy must be given within 7 days of a written request (reg 30(2)) only appears in later versions, Authorised Versions 005 and 009 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I couldn't confirm its wording in Version 002.
- **The Act itself.** The only retrieved copy is Authorised Version 115 (dated 13 October 2026), which wasn't in force in 2023 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So I haven't relied on its sections for this answer.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered: the answer says 'No minimum number of circuits' and that the retrieved documents 'had no rule on how many circuits a rental needs.' For next steps it advises reporting the problem in writing to request repairs, describes the urgent-repair route, and says to 'Ask when the last electrical safety check was done.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer states "No minimum number of circuits" and that the circuit breaker/RCD rule "wasn't in force yet" because it applies "On and from 29 March 2023", so it asserts neither failure condition.

version-cited.reason: No: the answer names the Regulations correctly as "Authorised Version 002", but it never names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 in the version in force on 1 March 2023 (Authorised Version No. 101). It identifies only "Authorised Version 115 (dated 13 October 2026)" while still discussing urgent repairs under section 3(1) of the Act, so a required document is missing its in-force version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
# Can a rooming house charge for coin-operated washing machines? (as at 15 October 2026)

**Short answer:** The documents I found don't directly say whether coin-operated washing machines are allowed or banned in a rooming house. Nothing in them forbids charging for laundry. They do set rules on how operators charge for services and how many washing machines they must provide.

**Version used:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 115** (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", in force from 13 October 2026). This is the version that applies on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

---

## What the law says

**1. Charging for services (s 109).** If an operator charges you for services, they must:
- give you a **separate schedule of the amounts** for those services **before you move in**, and
- if you use any of those services, give you an **itemised account showing your own use** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The Act assumes operators can charge for services, as long as they follow these rules. It doesn't name laundry or coin machines specifically.

**2. Metered utilities (s 108).** This section only lets operators charge for **electricity, gas and water used in your room**, if your room is separately metered. The charge can't be more than the supplier charges [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It doesn't cover shared washing machines.

**3. Public and community housing (s 109A).** If your operator is **Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency**, it may charge a service charge for **laundry** facilities, but only if it's "not possible or practicable to accurately measure" your use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The charge **must not exceed the cost of providing the service**. You must get written notice of the charge or any change to it, and you can ask the Tribunal to withdraw or change it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say how this applies to coin machines, which do measure each use.

**4. Minimum laundry standard.** Under the *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023*, **Authorised Version No. 002** (in force from 1 December 2024), the rule from **26 February 2024** is that operators must provide, in good working order, **for every 12 or fewer residents** (counting the most residents the house can hold) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf):
- a communal laundry trough or basin with hot and cold water
- a space with hot and cold water outlets for a washing machine
- a clothes line or other drying facility
- **a washing machine**

The regulations say a washing machine must be **provided**, but not whether it must be free. I can't confirm Version 002 is still the latest on 15 October 2026. It's simply the most recent version I found.

---

## What you can do

- **Ask for the services schedule.** You can check whether you were given a schedule of laundry charges before you moved in, and ask for an itemised account of your use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Count the machines.** Two machines meet the standard for a house that can hold up to 24 residents. If the house can hold more than 24, ask the operator about it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).
- **If the operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency,** you can ask for written details of any laundry charge, check it isn't more than the cost of providing the service, and apply to the Tribunal to withdraw or change it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **If a machine breaks down or a house rule seems unfair:** the earlier **Version No. 111** (in force 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026) required operators to keep facilities and equipment **in good repair** (s 120). It also let residents ask the Tribunal to declare a house rule **unreasonable** (s 128) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I didn't find these sections in the Version 115 text, so I can't confirm their current wording.

For a definite answer about coin-operated machines in your house, you could contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy legal service.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The hardest one, that the law doesn't say the machines must be free, is covered by 'The regulations say a washing machine must be **provided**, but not whether it must be free.' The answer also states that operators must provide a working washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents, that charges for services must be set out in a schedule given before moving in, and that the reader can check whether they were given a schedule of laundry charges before moving in.

The answer says the regulations require a washing machine to be "provided, but not whether it must be free", and that "Nothing in them forbids charging for laundry". It states the Act does "set rules on how operators charge for services" through the s 109 schedule and itemised account. It limits the cost cap to cases where "your operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency".

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
# Mouldy photos in a rental ad: Victorian law on 1 October 2025

**Versions in force on 1 October 2025:**
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110** (in force 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 004** (in force 1 July 2025 to 24 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

---

## What the law says

**1. Mould is covered by the minimum standards.** Under Schedule 4, clause 8 of the Regulations (Version 004), "each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure." [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

**2. Advertising a place that doesn't meet the standards.** A rule on this exists, but the copy of Version 110 I found doesn't include it.
- The rule is section 65B. It says a rental provider or agent "must not advertise or otherwise offer premises to let unless at the time the premises are advertised or otherwise offered to let, the residential rental provider or the provider's agent reasonably believes the premises comply with the rental minimum standards." The penalty is 60 penalty units for an individual and 300 for a company. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- I found this text only in a **later** document, Version 111, which started on 25 November 2025. It notes that s 65B was inserted by Act No. 6/2025 s. 16. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- So I can't confirm from the documents that s 65B applied on 1 October 2025.
- Even where s 65B applies, the test is whether the provider or agent **reasonably believed** the place complied when they advertised it. The place doesn't actually have to comply for them to meet that test. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- In later versions, a duty to keep records showing compliance with s 65B was added (s 65E, from Act No. 46/2025). That section doesn't appear in Version 111, so it wasn't in force on 1 October 2025. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

**3. Is the photo enough to prove a breach? The documents don't say.** None of them deal with what evidence proves a breach. A photo on its own may also fall short of what clause 8 requires. The standard isn't just "no mould". It covers mould and damp "caused by or related to the building structure." [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) A photo can show mould, but not necessarily what's causing it.

---

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask the agent directly** whether the property meets the minimum standards and whether there's mould in that bedroom. Ask about the cause too. The Act requires providers to disclose prescribed information before you sign a lease (s 30D(e)). [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) I found that section only in older versions (2021 and 2022). The list of what must be disclosed comes from a **later** version of the Regulations (Version 005, from 25 November 2025). It includes whether the place meets the minimum standards and any repair notice in the last 3 years about mould or damp caused by the building structure. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) I can't confirm that list from Version 004.
- **If you sign but haven't moved in yet:** under Version 110 (s 91L(f)), you can end the agreement before moving in by giving notice that the premises "do not meet any rental minimum standards." [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **If you move in and the mould is there:** the provider must make sure the place meets the minimum standards on or before your move-in day. If it doesn't, you can ask for urgent repairs (s 65A). The provider also has to keep the property in good repair whether or not you knew about the problem before moving in (s 68(1A)). [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) I found both sections only in Version 111 (from 25 November 2025), so check that they applied on your date.
- **Keep the ad and the photos** as a record of what was shown. The documents don't say how much weight a photo carries as evidence.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
# Getting a friend out of your rental (Victoria, as at 15 October 2026)

**In short:** The documents I have explain the risk this creates for your own tenancy. They don't set out the steps a renter must follow to remove a person they let move in. I can't tell you the exact process from these sources.

**Version applied:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version **115** (rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, in force from 13 October 2026). This was the version in force on your date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

---

## What the law says about your situation

- **You needed written consent.** You must not sub-let all or part of the property without the rental provider's written consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **An unauthorised sub-letting is invalid.** It is invalid unless the Tribunal (VCAT) has decided consent wasn't needed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **This puts your tenancy at risk.** If you have sub-let, or tried to sub-let, without consent, the rental provider may give *you* a notice to vacate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That notice must give a termination date **at least 14 days** after it is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Whether your friend legally counts as a "sub-tenant" or is just an occupant depends on things like whether they pay you rent. The documents don't settle that question for your facts.

---

## What you can do or ask

1. **Expect no help from the documents on removing your friend.** The parts of Version 115 I found don't describe a notice, notice period or VCAT application for a renter to remove someone they let move in.
2. **Don't try to force them out.** An older version (Version 101, from 2022) makes it an offence for a rental provider to force a renter out, or take possession, "except in accordance with this Act." The penalty is 150 penalty units for an individual [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). I couldn't confirm that this section is the same in Version 115. Whether it applies to you as the renter is also unclear.
3. **Know what happens if you end your own lease.** Version 101 also says that if a sub-tenant stays on after the main lease ends, they can become the rental provider's renter [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Again, I couldn't check this against Version 115.
4. **Get advice.** An earlier version of the official notice-to-vacate form points renters to Consumer Affairs Victoria (consumer.vic.gov.au/renting, **1300 558 181**). It also says only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only under a VCAT warrant [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That form was in force until 9 February 2026, so check it's still current.

**Bottom line:** Ask Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy legal service what notice or VCAT process applies to your friend before you act.

The hardest point is also covered, since the answer says it depends on the arrangement and names a deciding fact: 'Whether your friend legally counts as a "sub-tenant" or is just an occupant depends on things like whether they pay you rent.'

It advises "Don't try to force them out" rather than suggesting a lockout or removing belongings. It does not say the friend lacks rights, and notes a sub-tenant "can become the rental provider's renter." It never says the friend can simply apply to VCAT to be added to the lease.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
On 1 November 2019, Victorian law says a notice to vacate given **without a reason** has **no effect** if it was given in response to a tenant using, or proposing to use, a right under the Act. You can challenge it at the Tribunal, but you must apply **no later than 60 days after the notice was given**.

**Which law applies:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version 088** (file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf", dated 2 July 2019). It was in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The next version, 089, only started on 4 December 2019 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). Version 088 also prints later amendments in its endnotes, using terms like "renter" and "residential rental provider". Those weren't yet in force, so I haven't used them.

---

## What the law says

**A notice for no specified reason (s 263)**
- A landlord can give a notice to vacate without giving a reason [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- For a periodic (month-to-month) tenancy, the termination date must be at least **120 days** after the notice is given. If your tenancy is the type covered by s 230(3A), it is a prescribed period, or 120 days if none is prescribed [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**Retaliation (s 266(2))**
- A notice under s 263, or under s 261 (end of a fixed term), "is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the tenant of a right under this Act" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- This protection only covers s 261 and s 263 notices in this version [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**Time limit (s 266(3)(c))**
- You can't apply to the Tribunal to challenge a s 263 notice "after the end of 60 days after the date on which the notice is given" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**Excessive rent orders (s 265)**
- A landlord can't give a s 263 notice while an excessive rent order under s 47 is in force [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- If such an order is made before the termination date, the notice becomes invalid from the date of the order [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**If the notice says it's for repairs (s 255)**
- A repairs notice is only allowed if all three of these apply [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf):
  - the landlord intends to repair, renovate or reconstruct the premises;
  - the landlord has obtained all necessary permits and consents; and
  - the work can't be done properly unless you move out.
- The termination date must be at least **60 days** after the notice is given [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The ban on re-letting for 6 months only covers notices under ss 256–259, not s 255 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover:**
- They don't include the sections on tenants' repair rights. So I can't confirm from them that following up repairs counts as "a right under this Act".
- They don't include the rules on the required form of a notice in this version.
- They don't say how the Tribunal decides whether a notice was "in response to" something, or who has to prove it.

---

## What you can do or check

1. **Find out which section the notice relies on.**
   - If it gives no reason (s 263), the retaliation protection can apply [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - If it gives a reason, such as repairs, check whether that ground's conditions are actually met. For repairs, that means permits, genuine intended work, and a need for you to leave [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the termination date.** For a month-to-month tenancy, a s 263 notice needs at least 120 days [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If it was given on 1 November 2019, that is no earlier than about 29 February 2020 (my calculation).
3. **Check for an excessive rent order.** Is a s 47 order in force or being sought? If so, a s 263 notice can't be given, or becomes invalid [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Keep evidence of timing.** Keep your repair requests and follow-ups, with dates, and the notice itself. The notice arriving the same day as your follow-up is relevant to whether it was "in response to" you using your rights [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Apply to the Tribunal in time.** The deadline is the end of 60 days after the notice was given [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For a notice given on 1 November 2019, that is about **31 December 2019** (my calculation). Applying earlier is safer.

Questions to ask:
- Ask the landlord in writing which section the notice is given under.
- If it's for repairs, ask for proof of the permits and consents.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Short answer:** You may be able to challenge it, but it depends on facts you can't confirm yet. On 1 October 2025 the Act banned an agent from *inviting* bids above the advertised rent. It did **not** yet ban *accepting* a higher offer that nobody asked for.

**Law in force on 1 October 2025:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 110** ("rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025, in force 6 August to 24 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

---

## What the law said

**1. The rent had to be a fixed amount.** A rental provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is a fixed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A sign at the property that shows no rent is an exception [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**2. Inviting higher offers was banned.** A provider or agent "must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Penalty: **60 penalty units** (individual) or **300 penalty units** (company) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**3. Accepting an unprompted higher offer was not yet banned.** Section 30F(4) makes it an offence to accept "an unsolicited or otherwise uninvited" higher offer. It appears only in the later **Authorised Version No. 111** (dated 25 November 2025), inserted by Act No. 6/2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). It is not in Version No. 110 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). So the key question is whether the agent **invited** the higher offer.

**4. Misleading rent advertising.** A provider or agent advertising a property must not make a false or misleading statement about the rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Misleading conduct that persuades someone to sign a lease is also banned [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Both rules apply only to providers or agents "not acting in trade or commerce" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). They don't limit the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**5. Relisting at a higher rent.** I found nothing in Version No. 110 that bans relisting at a new, higher fixed price. It could matter if it shows the first advertised rent was misleading [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**6. The false "you withdrew" email.** None of the documents I found deal with an agent falsely saying an applicant withdrew. I can't say from the documents whether that, on its own, breaks the Act.

---

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask the agent in writing** why your application was recorded as withdrawn, and whether they asked anyone for an offer above the advertised rent. That second point is what matters under s 30F(3) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Where to complain:** the documents for this period don't set out a complaint or enforcement process. The Act mentions Tribunal orders for breaches of s 30E, but the text of that section (s 472(1A)) wasn't in the results [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Compensation under s 210AA covers loss from **discrimination** only [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). That would apply only if you think a personal attribute was the reason, which you haven't mentioned.

---

## Evidence to save

The documents don't list what evidence to keep. These suggestions are my own, based on what would need to be proven:

- **The original listing** (screenshots with date and URL), showing the fixed advertised rent.
- **Your application** and any confirmation it was received.
- **The "withdrawn" email** in full, with sender, date and time.
- **Proof you never withdrew**, such as your sent messages and call logs.
- **The new listing** at the higher rent, with date and URL.
- **Anything showing the agent asked for or encouraged higher offers**, such as messages, inspection notes, or the name of the person who told you, and what they heard and when. Hearsay is weaker evidence, so try to get it confirmed in writing.
- **Your own notes** of every conversation, made as soon as possible afterwards.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
# Can they refuse your dog request? Probably not by just saying no.

The law in force on 15 October 2026 is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115** ("rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **The owner can't unreasonably refuse.** A rental provider "must not unreasonably refuse to consent to the renter keeping a pet on the rented premises" (s 71C(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Saying no isn't enough.** The provider is taken to have consented unless they apply to VCAT under s 71D **within 14 days** of getting your request (s 71C(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Under s 71D(1), they can ask VCAT for an order that refusing is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your timing matters.** You sent the approved form (required by s 71B) three weeks ago [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That's more than 14 days. **If the owner didn't apply to VCAT within 14 days, the law treats them as having consented**, even though the agent said no.
- **The allergy is for VCAT to weigh.** The documents don't say whether an owner's allergy is a good enough reason to refuse. They also say nothing about how often the owner visits. If the case goes to VCAT, it can consider the type of pet, the nature of the property and its fixtures, whether another Act allows the refusal, any prescribed matters, and "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant" (s 71E(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT can then either let you keep the pet, or decide the refusal is reasonable and exclude the pet (s 71E(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

One caveat: you sent the request about three weeks ago, so the 14 days ran mostly under an earlier version of the Act. I don't have that version (the versions I have are No. 110, No. 111 and No. 115). The pet sections are the same in No. 110 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), No. 111 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and No. 115 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), but I can't confirm the version in force in between.

## What you can do

1. **Ask the agent in writing** whether the owner applied to VCAT within 14 days of getting your request.
2. **Keep proof of the date you gave the request**, since the 14 days run from then [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If no VCAT application was made in time**, you can point to s 71C(2): consent is deemed to have been given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **If an application was made**, VCAT decides. You can argue the allergy isn't a reasonable ground because the owner rarely visits. The documents don't say how VCAT would rule on that.
5. **Don't ignore an exclusion order.** If VCAT orders the pet out and you haven't complied at least 14 days after the order takes effect, the owner can give you a notice to vacate with at least 28 days' notice (s 91ZZG) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
